title: He Carried the Unclean Too: The Scandal Inside the Ark That Nobody Talks About
paragraphs: He Carried the Unclean Too: The Scandal Inside the Ark That Nobody Talks About
Why did Noah bring both clean and unclean animals—and what it exposes about the way God saves people who still feel unworthy?
It doesn’t make sense at first.
If God was starting over… if the flood was judgment… if the ark was meant to preserve what was pure… then why didn’t He only save what was clean?
Why carry the unclean into a new beginning?
Why preserve what didn’t belong?
And if you’re honest… that question hits deeper than animals.
Because somewhere inside you, there’s something you’ve labeled unclean.
Something you think God should have left behind.
Something you’re surprised He hasn’t exposed, judged, or erased yet.
And that’s where this story stops being about Noah… and starts becoming about you.
Genesis doesn’t hide it. It says it plainly, almost uncomfortably:
“Of clean animals you shall take seven pairs… and of the animals that are not clean, two…” (Genesis 7:2)
In Hebrew, the word for clean is טָהוֹר (tahor)—pure, acceptable, ceremonially fit.
The word for unclean is טָמֵא (tame’)—defiled, impure, unfit for worship.
God didn’t accidentally include both.
He commanded it.
Let that settle.
Before the Law of Moses… before dietary rules… before temple sacrifices were fully revealed… God already made a distinction between what was clean and unclean.
And yet…
He didn’t eliminate the unclean.
He preserved it.
He carried it through judgment.
He brought it into the future.
Why?
Because God’s plan has never been about only saving what looks righteous.
It has always been about transforming what isn’t.
The ark was not a museum of perfection.
It was a vessel of mercy.
And mercy, by definition, carries what justice could have destroyed.
Think about that.
Inside that ark, breathing the same air, standing on the same ground, were animals that symbolized purity… and animals that symbolized impurity.
Together.
Not separated.
Not filtered.
Not excluded.
Saved.
That should disturb something in your theology.
Because some of us have built a version of God that only makes room for the “tahor” parts of our lives.
The clean prayers.
The polished behavior.
The visible obedience.
But the hidden parts?
The thoughts you don’t say out loud.
The habits you’re still fighting.
The shame you think disqualifies you.
You assume those parts would never be invited onto the ark.
But Scripture says otherwise.
God didn’t wait for everything to become clean before He saved it.
He saved it knowing it wasn’t.
And if that doesn’t shake you, it should.
Because Noah didn’t purify the animals before bringing them in.
He simply obeyed God and brought what God commanded.
That means the ark carried tension.
It carried contradiction.
It carried the reality that salvation begins before transformation is complete.
And then something even more revealing happens.
After the flood subsides, Noah steps out, and the first recorded act of worship is this:
“Then Noah built an altar to the LORD… and took some of every clean animal… and offered burnt offerings…” (Genesis 8:20)
Notice carefully.
Only the clean animals were sacrificed.
Not the unclean.
Why does that matter?
Because the clean animals were set apart for atonement.
They pointed forward to something greater.
To Someone greater.
In Hebrew sacrificial language, these offerings were a shadow of substitution—something pure given in place of something not.
And that shadow finds its fulfillment in Jesus Christ.
When John the Baptist saw Him, he didn’t say, “Behold, a teacher” or “Behold, a prophet.”
He said, “Behold, the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world” (John 1:29).
In Greek, ὁ ἀμνὸς τοῦ Θεοῦ (ho amnos tou Theou)—the Lamb of God.
A clean sacrifice.
Given for the unclean.
Suddenly, the ark makes sense.
God preserved both clean and unclean because His plan was never to destroy the unclean completely…
but to redeem it through sacrifice.
You were never meant to clean yourself up before coming to Him.
You were meant to come as you are… and let the sacrifice do what you cannot.
That’s the scandal.
That’s the part religion struggles to accept.
Because it’s easier to manage behavior than to surrender brokenness.
But God didn’t design salvation to be behavior management.
He designed it to be resurrection.
And resurrection always begins with something that looks dead, broken, or beyond repair.
So if you’ve been sitting there thinking, “I don’t belong in something holy…”
You’re right.
On your own, you don’t.
But the ark was never about worthiness.
It was about obedience to God’s invitation.
And the cross was never about rewarding the clean.
It was about rescuing the unclean.
Be honest.
How many times have you disqualified yourself from God’s presence because of something you couldn’t fix?
How many times have you thought, “Once I get my life together, then I’ll come back”?
That’s not the Gospel.
That’s delay disguised as humility.
God already made provision for what you’re still struggling with.
Romans 5:8 says, “But God demonstrates His love toward us, in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us.”
Not after you fixed yourself.
Not after you became “tahor.”
While you were still “tame’.”
Still messy.
Still inconsistent.
Still wrestling.
He made a way.
And if Noah had refused to bring the unclean animals onto the ark…
those species would have been lost.
Gone.
Erased from the future.
Let that sink in.
If you keep trying to hide or reject the parts of you that need God the most…
you’re resisting the very mercy that was designed to carry you through.
God isn’t shocked by your struggle.
He accounted for it.
He made room for it.
But He refuses to leave it unchanged.
That’s the difference.
Grace includes you…
but it doesn’t leave you the same.
That’s why the story doesn’t end in the ark.
It moves toward sacrifice.
And ultimately toward Jesus.
Because only Christ can take what is unclean and make it new.
2 Corinthians 5:17 says, “If anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation.”
The old doesn’t get managed.
It gets replaced.
That’s the promise.
That’s the hope.
That’s the invitation.
So here’s the real question:
Are you still standing outside the ark because you think you’re too unclean to enter?
Or are you willing to trust that God already knew… and still made room for you?
Be honest.
This hit deeper than you expected.
If you truly want to glorify God, don’t just feel this—help carry it.
Let someone else encounter the same truth that just found you.
And if you’re ready to go deeper… to actually grow, not just feel inspired for a moment…
This isn’t about content.
It’s about transformation.
Because the same God who told Noah to carry the unclean…
is the same God who refused to leave you behind.
And He’s still calling you in.
You don’t have to be clean to come.
But you will never stay the same if you do.
